name: Dense data
summary: Compact, exact and quiet, for analysts who scan alerts and compare signals all day.
description: Dense data is an Open DS scheme: a full set of answers to the Open DS grammar, with the reasons behind each, usage rules, voice and tone, and the tokens that follow. Compact, exact and quiet, for analysts who scan alerts and compare signals all day.

ai.use_when: Security operations, threat detection, model monitoring, admin panels and analytics: many records, daily expert users, mouse and keyboard.
ai.avoid_when: Public sites, reading products, or first-time visitors on phones.

answers.why: IBM Plex Sans for every text role and IBM Plex Mono for data: exact and quiet, so the numbers stay the hero.

considers.readability: Plex Sans is a neutral grotesque with open shapes, made for screens; it reads at the small body size dense rows need.
considers.legibility: Data, codes and IDs sit in Plex Mono, where each character holds its own fixed cell, so they read character by character.
considers.scalability: Plex ships a full range of weights, so every role in the type scale has its own weight without a second sans.
considers.numerals: Digits in Plex Mono are all one width, so columns of numbers line up.
considers.scripts: Plex Sans covers Latin, Cyrillic and Greek; Hebrew, Arabic and other scripts come as sister families of IBM Plex, drawn to match.
considers.recognition: One family with a matching mono gives the product an engineered, consistent voice.
considers.familiarity: A grotesque reads as standard and trusted in operations tools.
considers.personality: Precise, as the brand answer asks, and quiet, so the brand steps back.
considers.performance: Two families; load only the weights the scale uses.
considers.licensing: SIL Open Font License: free to embed in apps and on the web.
considers.fallback: Falls back to system-ui and ui-monospace, as its tokens say; Plex Mono is its own pair.

default.label: Dense data
default.description: The single brand: precise blue on cool grey.

theme.$description: The Dense data theme: what each brand-dependent semantic key picks, in light and dark, plus mode-free picks (fonts, corners) in base. Info uses blue, kept apart from the brand color so it never reads as an action. Categories 1 to 5 are violet, blue, green, amber, slate: distinct hues for tags and chart series, with no meaning. Disabled uses the neutral slate.

open-ds.why: radius.2: We use a 2px corner for buttons and inputs in order to mark their role as controls and keep density. A small radius does this by softening the edge just enough to read as an object, while it keeps straight lines that align in rows. So a dense toolbar reads as one line of actions, because the product is dense (content.q2) and precise (brand.q1), with slightly rounded controls (shape.values).

radius.0: We use a square corner for badges in order to give status a role of its own, apart from the 2px controls. A zero radius does this by keeping the badge a plain rectangle with no curve. So status badges line up down a table column, because badges get their own corner (shape.roles) and people scan and compare rows (tasks.q1).

radius.0: We use a square corner for menu options in order to keep nesting by the relation: the 4px surface corner minus the panel's 4px padding. The inner radius does this by following the outer curve at the padding's distance, and here no curve is left. So an option's edge runs parallel to its menu's edge, because surfaces take 4px (shape.roles, brand.q1) and the layout is compact (spacing.values).

radius.2: We use the 2px control corner for boxes that grow in order to keep their role, as objects of one family, by inheritance from the control corner. The same radius does this by giving a list row or a text area the curve of the controls beside it. So rows and fields read as one family, because the control corner is small, not a pill (shape.values), and the product is dense (content.q2).

radius.4: We use a 4px corner for cards, menus and dialogs in order to make touching panels read as separate objects, in a precise tone by brand convention. A small radius does this by breaking the outline at each corner, just softer than the 2px controls. So panels read apart yet still tile neatly, because containers get their own corner (shape.roles, shape.count) and the brand is precise (brand.q1).

So a menu reads as above the grid without a heavy edge, because only what floats rises (elevation.roles) and shadows are subtle (elevation.values).

shadow.none: We use the light pick for the dark card elevation in order to keep the height it sets, and the step does this by the same means, so the dark card elevation and the light pick never differ, because the step reads the same in dark (theming.values).

shadow.overlay-dark: We use the light shadow's shape for menus and dialogs in dark in order to show the same floating height by the dark-shade relation. The cast shade does this by the same 8px offset and 24px blur, at 50% black instead of 16%. So a menu still lifts off the dark page, though its shade reads weaker on dark than in light, because only what floats rises (elevation.roles) and dark ships as standard (theming.values).

neutral.why: Muted color keeps attention on the data; a cool gray reads as precise.

open-ds.why: Small steps on a 4px grid give a 4px base. Compact density keeps the multiples low: parts of one item sit one step apart, groups four and sections six.

We use 4px for the tight gap between the parts of one item, such as an icon and its word, in order to group and separate: one base step (1 × 4px), the smallest gap on the 4px grid. Distance does this by grouping what is near and separating what is far, as the eye reads proximity (Gestalt), so a gap between groups stays clearly larger than a gap inside one. So each item in a dense row reads as one unit, because steps are small, on a 4px grid (spacing.definition), and the layout is compact (spacing.values).

We use 8px for the default gap between the items of one group in order to group and separate: two base steps (2 × 4px), twice the tight gap. Distance does this by the rule given for space.gap.tight, so analysts tell one record from the next while a list stays close, because the layout is compact (spacing.values) and experts want a lot on one screen (content.q2).

We use 16px for the group gap between groups in a layout in order to group and separate: four base steps (4 × 4px), four tight gaps. Distance does this by the rule given for space.gap.tight, so a new group starts without pushing records off the screen, because the layout is compact (spacing.values) and people must keep their place (human.q1).

We use 24px for the section gap between page sections in order to group and separate: six base steps (6 × 4px), half again the group gap. Distance does this by the rule given for space.gap.tight, so sections part with a hairline and little space, and the data keeps the room, because the layout is compact (spacing.values) and experts want a lot on one screen (content.q2).

We use 12px for the inline padding inside controls in order to give content room inside its box: three base steps (3 × 4px), the same as a table cell. Padding does this by keeping content off the edge of its box, so the content reads as part of that box, and by setting the size of the box with the content. So buttons stay short and a toolbar holds every action an expert repeats, because actions repeat constantly (tasks.q2) and the layout is compact (spacing.values).

We use 16px for the padding inside cards and dialogs in order to give content room inside its box: four base steps (4 × 4px), the same as the group gap. Padding does this by the rule given for space.inset.control-x, so content starts close to the edge of its box, because experts want a lot on one screen (content.q2) and the layout is compact (spacing.values).

We use 12px for the inline padding inside table cells in order to give content room inside its box: three base steps (3 × 4px), the same as a control. Padding does this by the rule given for space.inset.control-x, so more columns fit, and values in two columns still stay apart, because people scan and compare rows (tasks.q1) and the layout is compact (spacing.values).
A pointer target sets the 32px default. Compact is one 8px step below it; large equals the default, as the scheme has no hero action. Rows are a decision of their own and stay one control tall.

default.$description: Height of buttons and inputs, and the smallest target.

open-ds.why: We use 32px for buttons and inputs in order to make a hit target: the pointer target size, step 0 of the control scale, a 32px hit area above the 24px WCAG 2.5.8 floor. Height does this by setting the hit area a finger or a pointer must hit; WCAG measures the hit area, not the drawn box (2.5.8: 24px at AA; 2.5.5: 44px at AAA), and padding or a label can make it larger than the box. So every control fits a mouse and toolbars stay short, because the smallest target is compact, for a pointer (accessibility.values), and experts work at a desk (scenarios.q1).

We use 24px for compact controls, such as a clear button inside a field, in order to make a hit target: one 8px step below the 32px default on the control scale, a 24px hit area that is exactly the WCAG 2.5.8 floor at AA, with no margin. Height does this by the rule given for size.control.default, so a small button fits inside a field, and the field keeps its row height, because the smallest target is compact, for a pointer (accessibility.values), and experts use a mouse at a desk (scenarios.q1).

large.$description: Height of large controls. Not used in this system, so it equals the default.

open-ds.why: We use 32px for large controls in order to make a hit target: the default's step on the control scale and the default's 32px hit area, as the scheme has no hero action. Height does this by the rule given for size.control.default, so toolbar buttons stay in line, and color and place mark the main action, because actions take three emphasis levels with one primary per view (color.count), and the smallest target is compact (accessibility.values).

We use 32px for one table row in order to keep the eye on its row: a row one 32px default control tall and no more, as rows are a decision of their own here and a row holds controls. Row height does this by making each row a band the eye follows across, and a hit target when the row is clickable (WCAG 2.5.8: 24px). So more records fit, and a control in a row fills its height, because row heights are a spacing role (spacing.roles) and the layout is compact (spacing.values).
16px icons match the small text, so an icon and its label in a toolbar read as one line.

hit-area.$description: The least hit area of a control. A control drawn smaller keeps its size; its hit area grows past it, never into a neighbour.

open-ds.why: We use a 24px hit area for controls drawn smaller, such as a 16px checkbox, in order to make a hit target at the WCAG 2.5.8 floor. The hit area does this by growing past the drawn box through a pseudo-element, while the control keeps its drawn size and rows in a group stand far enough apart that no two targets overlap. So experts hit a checkbox in a dense row with a mouse on the first try, because the smallest target is compact, for a pointer (accessibility.values), and the layout is compact (spacing.values).

badge.$description: Corner of badges, chips, tooltips, keyboard keys (kbd) and checkboxes: small labels and marks.

option.$description: Corner of options in menus and lists: the panel's corner less its padding, so the corners nest.

element.$description: Corner of an element that holds content and can grow past one line: a list item, an accordion row, a text area, a calendar, an attachment, a skeleton or media.

surface.$description: Corner of cards, menus and dialogs.

open-ds.why: We use a 1px default line for dividers and card borders in order to give separation between rows. A thin stroke does this by breaking the surface with the least weight a line can have; as a divider it decorates, so it has no contrast floor. So rows and cards stay apart without taking room from the data, because lines separate groups (elevation.definition) and AA is the floor (accessibility.definition).

width.$description: The focus ring's width: one step heavier than the default border, and not a border width.

open-ds.why: We use a 2px focus ring in order to show focus, one step heavier than the 1px default line by the focus relation. A heavier stroke does this by standing out from every border around it. So keyboard users always see which row has focus, because focus has its own look (accessibility.roles) and lines are thin (elevation.definition).

offset.$description: The gap between a control and its focus ring, so the ring never touches the control and reads on any fill.

open-ds.why: We use a fixed 2px focus offset in order to keep focus visible by contrast, not for style. The gap does this by showing the page color between ring and control, so one of the two colors keeps enough contrast against any fill (W3C technique C40). So keyboard users see the ring on any fill, even a selected row, because focus has its own look (accessibility.roles).

Few sizes: a small 14px body and a 1.2 ratio, each role on the next step, so every size is clearly apart and none is wasted. Short lines sit tight at 1.2. Body opens to 1.45, and data and captions sit snug at 1.3; their line boxes snap to a 2px grid, so rows of data keep whole-pixel lines.
24px is three ratio steps above the 14px body (14 × 1.2^3), the top of the scale, kept for the one key number on a dashboard. Everything below it stays small.
1.2, the tight step, because display holds one short number, not wrapped lines. The tight box keeps rows close below it.
600, the heaviest weight in the scale, makes the one display number the headline at a glance.
20px is two ratio steps above body and one under the 24px display, so page titles stay small and the table starts higher on the screen.
1.2, the tight step: a page title is one short line, so a tight box saves height above the table.
600 lets the small 20px title stand above the table by weight, not by a larger size.
16px sits one ratio step above the 14px body (14 × 1.2 = 16.8), snapped down to the 4px grid as headings are. Panel and card headings name a block without taking rows from the data.
1.2, the tight step for headings, keeps a panel heading in a short box, so the block below starts sooner.
600 separates a 16px heading from the 14px body by weight, because the two sit only one ratio step apart.
14px is the small body size and step 0 of the scale: every other role is a 1.2 ratio step from it, and more rows fit on the screen.
A 20px line box: the open step, 1.45 × 14px (20.3px), snapped to the 2px grid, because body is help text that wraps to several lines and rows of text keep the grid.
400, the regular weight, keeps help sentences quiet beside the data, so the brand steps back.

We use 12px for column headers and field labels in order to keep labels at the smallest legible step: one ratio step under the 14px body (14 ÷ 1.2), on the caption’s step. The size does this by keeping IBM Plex Sans’s x-height at 6.2px (0.516 of the em); at 11px it would drop to 5.7px. So a header repeats on every column without competing with the data, and still reads, because experts scan many records at a short reading distance (tasks.q1) and the type scale is small (typography.values).
1.2, the tight step for labels: a column header is one short name, so a 14.4px line keeps the header row low.
500 sets a 12px label apart from the 12px caption by weight alone, without a heavy 600 that competes with data.

We use 12px for timestamps and hints in order to let secondary text step back: one ratio step under the 14px body, the same step as label. The caption size does this by holding the lowercase letters of IBM Plex Sans at a 6.2px x-height, open enough to tell a 6 from a b at a glance. So experts read a timestamp across many rows while the values stay the hero, because the brand is quiet (brand.q2) and the content is numbers (content.q1).
A 16px line box for 12px captions: the snug step, 1.3 × 12px (15.6px), snapped to the 2px grid, so hints and timestamps that wrap stay on the grid.
400, the regular weight, so supporting text steps back behind the 500 labels and the data.
14px shares step 0 with body, so Plex Mono values read at the body size. The scale has no step between the 12px labels and 14px.

An 18px line box for 14px cells: the snug step, 1.3 × 14px (18.2px), snapped to the 2px grid. A cell holds one line, so the box sits just above the text: the eye keeps its row while it scans a long table, and the row stays dense.
400 keeps table values regular, so the mono digits stay even and columns compare at a glance.

feedback.$description: Hover, press and toggle feedback. At most 150ms in a productive family.

open-ds.why: We use 120ms (fast) for hover, press and toggle feedback in order to confirm each action inside the productive limit of 150ms. The duration does this by ending the change before the eye leaves the control. So experts see each action land and never wait for it, because motion is for feedback only, which makes the family productive (motion.roles), and feedback feels fast (motion.values).

panels.$description: Menus, popovers, dialogs and drawers opening. At most 300ms in a productive family.

open-ds.why: We use 120ms (fast) for menus, popovers, dialogs and other panels in order to show where a panel comes from, inside the productive limit of 300ms. The duration does this by giving the eye just enough frames to follow the panel from its trigger. So experts open a menu many times a shift and never wait for it, because the family is productive (motion.roles) and there is one speed (motion.count).

exit.$description: A layer closing. About 150ms, never more, in a productive family.

open-ds.why: We use the feedback duration, 120ms (fast), for a layer that closes in order to finish the exit move within the productive 150ms. The duration does this by removing the layer in fewer frames than an open takes, as nothing in it needs reading any more. So experts get the page back at once, because productive exits stay short (motion.roles) and there is one speed (motion.count).

standard.$description: The transition move: a state that changes in place, such as hover, press or toggle.

open-ds.why: We use the standard easing (0.2, 0, 0, 1) for state changes in place in order to do the transition move. The curve does this by reaching its target early and settling slowly, with no overshoot. So a hover, a press or a toggle lands at once and then stays still, because easing is a standard ease-out (motion.definition) and the family is productive (motion.roles).

enter.$description: The enter move: a layer that appears.

open-ds.why: We use the transition move's standard easing for a panel that appears in order to do the enter move. The curve does this by spending most of the change in the first frames, so the layer is in place before it slows. So experts can read a menu almost as soon as it opens, because easing is a standard ease-out (motion.definition) in a productive family (motion.roles).

exit.$description: The exit move: a layer that closes in place.

open-ds.why: We use the strong-out easing (0.23, 1, 0.32, 1) for a layer that closes in place in order to do the exit move of the productive family. The curve does this by covering most of the way in the first third of its time, then easing to a stop. So a closed popover is gone before the next click, because productive exits take a strong ease-out (motion.roles) and easing never springs here (motion.definition).

exit-offscreen.$description: The exit move of a layer that slides off the screen: a sheet or a drawer.

open-ds.why: We use the exit move's strong-out easing for a drawer or sheet that slides off the screen, in order to keep every exit of a productive family on one fast curve. The curve does this by moving fastest at the start, so the panel clears the view with no slow tail. So the content under a closing sheet comes back at once, because only an expressive family accelerates what leaves the screen (motion.roles), and easing is a plain ease-out (motion.definition).

emphasize.$description: The emphasize move: a moment that calls for attention.

open-ds.why: We use the transition move's standard easing for a moment that calls for attention in order to give the emphasize move no overshoot. The curve does this by stopping at its target without passing it. So a new message draws the eye by its change, not by a bounce, because the family is productive (motion.roles) and easing is a standard ease-out, never a spring (motion.definition).

neutral.$description: The neutral scale: the scheme's gray, step by step. Surfaces, borders and text read it, never a gray directly.

highlight.$description: The item the pointer or the keyboard is on.

pressed.$description: The item while it is pressed.

scrim.$description: Dims the page behind a dialog.

on-light.$description: Text on any light fill, in either mode.

on-dark.$description: Text on any dark fill, in either mode.

info-on-light.$description: Info text on a light info fill, such as its tint in light mode.

info-on-dark.$description: Info text on a dark info fill, such as its tint in dark mode.

success-on-light.$description: Success text on a light success fill, such as its tint in light mode.

success-on-dark.$description: Success text on a dark success fill, such as its tint in dark mode.

warning-on-light.$description: Warning text on a light warning fill, such as its tint in light mode.

warning-on-dark.$description: Warning text on a dark warning fill, such as its tint in dark mode.

danger-on-light.$description: Danger text on a light danger fill, such as its tint in light mode.

danger-on-dark.$description: Danger text on a dark danger fill, such as its tint in dark mode.

raised.$description: The 1px edge of a raised layer: menus, dialogs and toasts, and raised cards.

selected.$description: The edge that marks a selected item, so selection is never color alone.

@.$description: The fill of a destructive commit: the confirm of a delete.
Info text and icons: neutral news, no action needed.
Category 1: chart series, tag dots and icons. Tag text uses color.text.primary.
Category 2: chart series, tag dots and icons. Tag text uses color.text.primary.
Category 3: chart series, tag dots and icons. Tag text uses color.text.primary.
Category 4: chart series, tag dots and icons. Tag text uses color.text.primary.
Category 5: chart series, tag dots and icons. Tag text uses color.text.primary.

category.$description: Colors with no meaning, for content that needs telling apart: decorative accents and non-semantic blocks such as tags, labels and chart series.

disabled.$description: The shared look of controls that cannot be used right now.

text.$description: Text and icons of a disabled control.

open-ds.why: Compact: more records fit on one screen, so components keep their tightest spacing.

stroke-width.$description: The line weight of every icon, on Lucide's 24px grid.

open-ds.why: A 1.5px stroke width on Lucide's 24px grid keeps outline icons light, so they never outweigh the dense text beside them.

focus-ring-invalid.$description: Chips focus ring invalid of the combobox.
Focus ring invalid of the input group.
Slot focus ring invalid of the input otp.
Focus ring invalid of the native select.

radius.$description: Item radius of the radio group.
Group label radius of the sidebar.
Menu badge radius of the sidebar.
Menu skeleton radius of the sidebar.
Menu sub button radius of the sidebar.
Corner of the menu button, of the sidebar.
Corner of the switch's thumb: round, as the track is.

focus-ring-invalid.$description: Focus ring invalid of the textarea.

content.$description: Voice tokens: the words components use for common actions. Text, not CSS.

commit.$description: The label of the action that completes a task.

cancel.$description: The label of the way out next to the main action.

destroy.$description: The label of an action that deletes data.

retry.$description: The label that repeats a failed action.

empty-action.$description: The label of the action in an empty state.
